claim: The MET kinase domain variant library spans amino acid positions 1059-1345.
source: The MET kinase domain sequence used in this study spans amino acid positions 1059–1345, which includes the full kinase domain (aa 1071–1345) and a small region of the juxtamembrane (aa 1059–1070).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section describing the library construction.

claim: The variant DNA library was synthesized by Twist Bioscience containing one mammalian high-usage codon per amino acid.
source: The variant DNA library was synthesized by Twist Bioscience, containing one mammalian high-usage codon per amino acid.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: The library contains >99% of all possible 5764 kinase domain mutations.
source: We used our previously published library harboring >99% of all possible 5764 kinase domain (1059-1345aa) mutations in a TPR-fusion background carrying either a wild-type MET or exon 14 skipped intracellular domain (Estevam et al., 2024; Figure 1E).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the library.

claim: Ba/F3 cells have undetectable expression of endogenous RTKs.
source: We employed the Ba/F3 cell line as our selection system due to its undetectable expression of endogenous RTKs and addiction to exogenous interleukin-3 (IL-3; Estevam et al., 2024).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citation support.

claim: Ba/F3 cells are addicted to exogenous interleukin-3 (IL-3).
source: We employed the Ba/F3 cell line as our selection system due to its undetectable expression of endogenous RTKs and addiction to exogenous interleukin-3 (IL-3; Estevam et al., 2024).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citation support.

claim: TPR-MET fusion generates IL-3-independent constitutive activity.
source: We used a TPR-MET fusion to generate IL-3-independent constitutive activity (Estevam et al., 2024).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citation support.

claim: Crizotinib is one of four FDA approved inhibitors for MET.
source: Thousands of compounds have been screened against the MET kinase domain, and while several have undergone clinical trials, currently four MET inhibitors have received FDA approval: crizotinib, cabozantinib, tepotinib, and capmatinib (Santarpia et al., 2021; Wang and Lu, 2023).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Four MET inhibitors have received FDA approval: crizotinib, cabozantinib, tepotinib, and capmatinib.
source: Thousands of compounds have been screened against the MET kinase domain, and while several have undergone clinical trials, currently four MET inhibitors have received FDA approval: crizotinib, cabozantinib, tepotinib, and capmatinib (Santarpia et al., 2021; Wang and Lu, 2023).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Type I inhibitors occupy the adenosine binding pocket and form hydrogen bonds with hinge region residues.
source: Type I inhibitors occupy the adenosine binding pocket, form hydrogen bonds with 'hinge' region residues, and favor an active conformation.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction describing inhibitor types.

claim: Type II inhibitors occupy the adenosine pocket and extend into an opening in the R-spine accessible in an inactive conformation.
source: Type II inhibitors also occupy the adenosine pocket but extend into an opening in the R-spine that is accessible in an inactive conformation (Arter et al., 2022; Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation and figure reference.

claim: Type I½ inhibitors combine features from both type I and type II inhibitors, engaging with both the adenosine pocket and the R-spine pocket.
source: Type I½ inhibitors combine features from both type I and type II inhibitors, engaging with both the adenosine pocket and the R-spine pocket (Arter et al., 2022; Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation and figure reference.

claim: Type III inhibitors are allosteric, non-ATP competitive inhibitors.
source: Finally, type III inhibitors are allosteric, non-ATP competitive inhibitors (Arter et al., 2022; Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation and figure reference.

claim: Type I MET inhibitors leverage pi-stacking interactions with Y1230 and salt-bridge formation between D1228 and K1110.
source: Type I MET inhibitors leverage pi-stacking interactions with Y1230 and salt-bridge formation between D1228 and K1110, and are further classified as type Ia or Ib based on whether they interact with solvent front residue G1163 (Cui, 2014; Fujino et al., 2019; Wang and Lu, 2023; Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations and figure reference.

claim: Type Ia inhibitors have a solvent-front interaction with G1163.
source: Here, we specifically define type Ia inhibitors as having a solvent-front interaction (Cui, 2014), which structurally classifies tepotinib and capmatinib as type Ia based on our analysis of experimental structures and inhibitor docked models (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), despite classification as type Ib in other studies (Brazel et al., 2022; Fujino et al., 2022; Recondo et al., 2020a).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations and figure references.

claim: Tepotinib and capmatinib are structurally classified as type Ia inhibitors based on analysis of experimental structures and inhibitor docked models.
source: Here, we specifically define type Ia inhibitors as having a solvent-front interaction (Cui, 2014), which structurally classifies tepotinib and capmatinib as type Ia based on our analysis of experimental structures and inhibitor docked models (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), despite classification as type Ib in other studies (Brazel et al., 2022; Fujino et al., 2022; Recondo et al., 2020a).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations and figure references.

claim: Tivantinib displayed equivalent inhibition regardless of IL-3 presence.
source: In contrast, tivantinib displayed equivalent inhibition regardless of IL-3, reinforcing that tivantinib has cytotoxicity effects unrelated to MET inhibition (Figure 2E) and underscores the sensitivity of the DMS in identifying direct protein-drug effects.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Tivantinib has cytotoxicity effects unrelated to MET inhibition.
source: In contrast, tivantinib displayed equivalent inhibition regardless of IL-3, reinforcing that tivantinib has cytotoxicity effects unrelated to MET inhibition (Figure 2E) and underscores the sensitivity of the DMS in identifying direct protein-drug effects.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Crizotinib only displayed an inhibitory effect under IL-3 withdrawal, highlighting a MET-dependent mode of action.
source: As expected, crizotinib only displayed an inhibitory effect under IL-3 withdrawal, highlighting a MET-dependent mode of action.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: The strong correlation of tivantinib with the DMSO control (r=0.93) suggested a MET-independent mode of action.
source: The strong correlation of tivantinib with the DMSO control (r=0.93) and low correlation with all other inhibitors suggested a MET-independent mode of action.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: D1228, Y1230, and G1163 are positions with the highest frequency of gain-of-function mutations for crizotinib.
source: Indeed, the highest frequency of gain-of-function mutations occurred at residues mediating direct drug-protein interactions, such as D1228, Y1230, and G1163.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: D1228N/H/V/Y, Y1230C/H/N/S, G1163R mutations have been noted in prior reports.
source: These sites, and many of the individual mutations, have been noted in prior reports, such as: D1228N/H/V/Y, Y1230C/H/N/S, G1163R (Fernandes et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023; Bahcall et al., 2022; Recondo et al., 2020a; Rotow et al., 2020; Fujino et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2017; Pecci et al., 2024).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with multiple citations.

claim: G1163 and D1228 are positions with the highest frequency of resistance mutations across all inhibitor types.
source: Two positions stood out with the highest frequency of resistance: G1163 and D1228 (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: G1163 is at the solvent front entrance of the active site.
source: Both sites are unsurprising due to their inhibitor interactions - G1163 is at the solvent front entrance of the active site and D1228 stabilizes an inactive conformation of the A-loop with an inhibitor bound (Cui, 2014; Recondo et al., 2020a; Fernandes et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations.

claim: D1228 stabilizes an inactive conformation of the A-loop with an inhibitor bound.
source: Both sites are unsurprising due to their inhibitor interactions - G1163 is at the solvent front entrance of the active site and D1228 stabilizes an inactive conformation of the A-loop with an inhibitor bound (Cui, 2014; Recondo et al., 2020a; Fernandes et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations.

claim: M1211 is a previously documented resistance site and a C-spine residue.
source: Located at the base of the active site, M1211 is a previously documented resistance site (Tiedt et al., 2011) and a C-spine residue (Estevam et al., 2024), which harbors a smaller number of resistance mutations for all inhibitor types within our analysis (Figure 6A).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations and figure reference.

claim: Y1230 was a hotspot for type I and I½ inhibitors, but not a major resistance site for type II inhibitors.
source: In contrast to these universal sites, Y1230 was a hotspot for type I and I ½ inhibitors, but not a major resistance site for type II inhibitors (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Y1230 stabilizes inhibitors through pi-stacking interactions.
source: This specificity can be rationalized based on the role of Y1230 in stabilizing inhibitors through pi-stacking interactions (Cui, 2014).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citation.

claim: F1200 and L1195 are hotspots for type II but not type I inhibitors.
source: In contrast, F1200 and L1195 (Bahcall et al., 2022; Recondo et al., 2020b), are both hotspots for type II but not type I inhibitors (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations and figure reference.

claim: F1200 and L1195 make direct contact with type II inhibitors, but not type I inhibitors.
source: Again, this effect can be rationalized structurally: both residues make direct contact with type II inhibitors, but not type I inhibitors.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: There were a total of 17 shared variants with resistance across all inhibitor types.
source: Across all inhibitor types, there were a total of 17 shared variants with G1163, D1228, and M1211 being the most common (Figure 6G).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: I1084 is enriched as a resistance site for type I inhibitors.
source: For example, I1084 is enriched as a resistance site for type I inhibitors, consistent with previous studies in hereditary papillary renal cell carcinomas (Guérin et al., 2023).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citation.

claim: I1084 is located at the solvent front of the phosphate-loop (P-loop) of the kinase N-lobe.
source: I1084 is located at the solvent front of the phosphate-loop (P-loop) of the kinase N-lobe (Figure 1A), which is responsible for stabilization of the ATP phosphate groups.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: L1142 is an R-spine residue enriched for type II inhibitor resistance.
source: In contrast, L1142, an R-spine residue, and L1140, which sits at the back of the ATP-binding pocket, are enriched for type II inhibitor resistance, consistent with their spatial locations (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: L1140 sits at the back of the ATP-binding pocket and is enriched for type II inhibitor resistance.
source: In contrast, L1142, an R-spine residue, and L1140, which sits at the back of the ATP-binding pocket, are enriched for type II inhibitor resistance, consistent with their spatial locations (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Cabozantinib maintained the lowest average correlation with all type I inhibitors.
source: Overall, cabozantinib maintained the lowest average correlation with all type I inhibitors, making it the most divergent type II inhibitor within our screen, and potentially offering the least overlap in resistance (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure references.

claim: 44 mutations were identified as having crizotinib resistance and cabozantinib sensitivity.
source: By statistically filtering mutations that are categorized as gain-of-function in one inhibitor, but loss-of-function in the other, a set of 44 mutations were identified as having crizotinib resistance and cabozantinib sensitivity, and 3 mutations with the opposite profile (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: 3 mutations were identified as having cabozantinib resistance and crizotinib sensitivity.
source: By statistically filtering mutations that are categorized as gain-of-function in one inhibitor, but loss-of-function in the other, a set of 44 mutations were identified as having crizotinib resistance and cabozantinib sensitivity, and 3 mutations with the opposite profile (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Y1093K shows a nearly 10-fold shift in crizotinib sensitivity with no difference in cabozantinib sensitivity compared to wild-type TPR-MET.
source: When comparing the dose-response of Y1093K to the wild-type TPR-MET kinase domain, Y1093K shows a nearly 10-fold shift in crizotinib sensitivity with no difference in cabozantinib sensitivity (Figure 7D).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: L1195M is refractory to all concentrations of cabozantinib tested, but still sensitive to crizotinib.
source: In comparing the dose-response of L1195M to the wild-type TPR-MET kinase domain, we find that L1195M is refractory to all concentrations of cabozantinib tested, but still sensitive to crizotinib (Figure 7D).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: ESM-1b predicts the fitness of variants in the untreated/DMSO condition (correlation 0.50) much better than it does for the inhibitor treated datasets (correlation 0.28).
source: We observed that ESM-1b, a protein language model (Rives et al., 2021), predicts the fitness of variants in the untreated/DMSO condition (correlation 0.50) much better than it does for the inhibitor treated datasets (correlation 0.28).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citation.

claim: The augmented XGBoost model improves the performance from 0.28 to 0.37 correlation.
source: The final model uses a subset of the features we tested and improves the performance from 0.28 to 0.37 (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: MET is an RTK and proto-oncogene implicated in the pathogenesis of gastric, renal, colorectal, and lung cancers.
source: MET is an RTK and proto-oncogene that has been implicated in the pathogenesis of gastric, renal, colorectal, and lung cancers (Frampton et al., 2015; Duplaquet et al., 2018; Wood et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Clinical reports have documented recurrent resistance mutations at positions D1228, Y1230, G1163, L1195 for MET.
source: Clinical reports following post-treatment outcomes have documented recurrent resistance mutations at positions such as D1228, Y1230, G1163, L1195 for MET (Fernandes et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2017; Recondo et al., 2020a; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The juxtamembrane domain is encoded by exon 14 in MET and serves an incompletely understood negative regulatory function in the kinase.
source: The juxtamembrane domain is encoded by exon 14 in MET, serves an incompletely understood negative regulatory function in the kinase (Ma et al., 2003) and is recurrently excluded in cancer by somatically encoded exon skipping mutations.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: The exon 14 juxtamembrane domain is recurrently excluded in cancer by somatically encoded exon skipping mutations.
source: The juxtamembrane domain is encoded by exon 14 in MET, serves an incompletely understood negative regulatory function in the kinase (Ma et al., 2003) and is recurrently excluded in cancer by somatically encoded exon skipping mutations.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: Time points were selected every two cell doublings over the course of four time points.
source: Time points were selected every two cell doublings over the course of four time points, and cells were split and maintained in the absence of IL-3 and presence of drug at IC50 for each inhibitor, including a DMSO control.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: Cells were maintained in the absence of IL-3 and presence of drug at IC50 for each inhibitor during the screen.
source: Time points were selected every two cell doublings over the course of four time points, and cells were split and maintained in the absence of IL-3 and presence of drug at IC50 for each inhibitor, including a DMSO control.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: All samples across all time points and replicates were prepared for next-generation sequencing in parallel and sequenced on the same Illumina NovaSeq 6000 flow cell.
source: All samples, across all time points and replicates, were prepared for next-generation sequencing (NGS) in parallel, and sequenced on the same Illumina NovaSeq 6000 flow cell to identify variant frequencies (Figure 1F).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Variant fitness scores were calculated using Rosace.
source: We then calculated variant fitness scores using Rosace (Rao et al., 2024; Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citation and figure references.

claim: Type II inhibitors displayed the greatest similarities to one another, with merestinib and the glesatinib analog having the highest correlation (r=0.93).
source: Type II inhibitors displayed the greatest similarities to one another, with merestinib and the glesatinib analog having the highest correlation (r=0.93) and cabozantinib and glesatinib analog showing the lowest (r=0.87; Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Cabozantinib and glesatinib analog showed the lowest correlation among type II inhibitors (r=0.87).
source: Type II inhibitors displayed the greatest similarities to one another, with merestinib and the glesatinib analog having the highest correlation (r=0.93) and cabozantinib and glesatinib analog showing the lowest (r=0.87; Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: AMG-458 displayed higher similarity to type II inhibitors than to type I.
source: While there was only one type I½ inhibitor, AMG-458, it displayed higher similarity to type II inhibitors than to type I, likely due to similar type II back pocket interactions with the kinase R-spine (Figure 1B; Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure references.

claim: Capmatinib displayed the lowest correlations among type I inhibitors, potentially due to difficulty in experimental overdosing due to its greater potency.
source: While type I inhibitors were also highly correlated, capmatinib stood out as an outlier, displaying the lowest correlations potentially due to difficulty in experimental overdosing due to its greater potency (Bahcall et al., 2022; Fujino et al., 2019; Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with citations and figure reference.

claim: Previously discovered resistance mutations are strongly shifted to a GOF distribution for the drugs where resistance is reported from treatment or experiment.
source: Overall, previously discovered mutations are strongly shifted to a GOF distribution for the drugs where resistance is reported from treatment or experiment; in contrast, the distribution is centered around neutral for those sites for other drugs not reported in the literature (Figure 4C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: H1094Y demonstrated slight sensitivity to glesatinib in the assay.
source: However, in our assay H1094Y demonstrated slight sensitivity to gelesatinib, suggesting that either resistance is linked to the exon14 deletion isoform, the L1195V mutation, or a cellular factor not modeled well by the BaF3 system.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: L1195 is an αE-helix position with previously recorded resistance (L1195V/F).
source: L1195 is an ⍺E-helix position with previously recorded resistance (L1195V/F), which our analysis further supports as a type II-only resistance hotspot (Figure 6A).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: Mutations like Met or Phe at position 1195 clash with the fluorophenyl moiety of cabozantinib.
source: Structurally, mutations like Met or Phe at 1195 clash with the fluorophenyl moiety of cabozantinib used to access and stabilize a deep, back pocket of the kinase in an inactive conformation, unlike crizotinib which occupies the solvent front and adenosine binding region of the ATP binding site.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: Y1093 is located in β2 of the N-lobe, at the roof of the ATP-binding site.
source: Interestingly, Y1093 is located in β2 of the N-lobe, at the roof of the ATP-binding site, and does not directly engage with crizotinib.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: Y1093 does not directly engage with crizotinib.
source: Interestingly, Y1093 is located in β2 of the N-lobe, at the roof of the ATP-binding site, and does not directly engage with crizotinib.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: Y1093K mutation potentially contributes to resistance by perturbing the packing of β1-β2 and altering the conformation of the ATP binding site in a manner that destabilizes crizotinib binding.
source: We speculate this mutation potentially contributes to resistance by perturbing the packing of β1-β2 and altering the conformation of the ATP binding site in a manner that destabilizes crizotinib binding.

claim: The DMS of the MET kinase domain was performed against a panel of 11 inhibitors.
source: Here, we explore the landscape of TKI resistance of the MET kinase domain against a panel of 11 inhibitors, utilizing our previously established platform (Estevam et al., 2024).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: The panel of inhibitors included six type I inhibitors (crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib, glumetinib, savolitinib, and NVP-BVU972).
source: To evaluate the response of MET mutations to different inhibitors, we selected six type I inhibitors (crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib, glumetinib, savolitinib, and NVP-BVU972), three type II inhibitors (cabozantinib, glesatinib analog, merestinib), and a proposed type III inhibitor, tivantinib (Figure 1C).

claim: The panel of inhibitors included three type II inhibitors (cabozantinib, glesatinib analog, merestinib).
source: To evaluate the response of MET mutations to different inhibitors, we selected six type I inhibitors (crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib, glumetinib, savolitinib, and NVP-BVU972), three type II inhibitors (cabozantinib, glesatinib analog, merestinib), and a proposed type III inhibitor, tivantinib (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section with figure reference.

claim: The panel of inhibitors included a proposed type III inhibitor, tivantinib.
source: To evaluate the response of MET mutations to different inhibitors, we selected six type I inhibitors (crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib, glumetinib, savolitinib, and NVP-BVU972), three type II inhibitors (cabozantinib, glesatinib analog, merestinib), and a proposed type III inhibitor, tivantinib (Figure 1C).

claim: Inhibitor-treated populations displayed distributions with a loss-of-function peak, representative of mutations that are sensitive to the inhibitor.
source: Also as expected, inhibitor-treated populations displayed distributions with a loss-of-function peak, representative of mutations that are sensitive to the inhibitor.

claim: Inhibitor populations were right-skewed, showing greater enrichment of gain-of-function scores at the positive tail of distributions.
source: Unlike DMSO, inhibitor populations were right-skewed, showing greater enrichment of gain-of-function scores at the positive tail of distributions (Figure 2A).

claim: Capmatinib showed the greatest difference from DMSO with a Pearson's correlation of 0.45.
source: These population differences were exemplified by the low correlation between each inhibitor and DMSO, with capmatinib showing the greatest difference from DMSO with a Pearson's correlation of 0.45, and tivantinib standing as an outlier with a Pearson's correlation of 0.93 (Figure 2B).

claim: Tivantinib showed a Pearson's correlation of 0.93 with DMSO, standing as an outlier.

claim: Tivantinib selectively targets an inactive DFG-motif conformation, with tivantinib stabilizing residues (F1089, R1227) blocking ATP binding.
source: In vitro assays on the purified MET kinase domain have shown that tivantinib has the potential to hinder catalytic activity (Munshi et al., 2010) and structural studies revealed that it selectively targets an inactive DFG-motif conformation, with tivantinib stabilizing residues (F1089, R1227) blocking ATP binding (Eathiraj et al., 2011; Figure 2D).

claim: Comparative MET-dependent and MET-independent cell-based studies on tivantinib have shown MET agnostic anti-tumor activity.
source: Yet in contradiction, comparative MET-dependent and MET-independent cell-based studies on tivantinib have also shown MET agnostic anti-tumor activity, posing that tivantinib may have an alternative inhibitory mechanism than an MET-selective one (Michieli and Di Nicolantonio, 2013; Basilico et al., 2013; Katayama et al., 2013; Fujino et al., 2019).

claim: Regions with sensitivity to crizotinib occurred throughout the kinase, primarily in loop-regions which have the greatest mutational tolerance in DMSO.

claim: I1084 is located in β1 at the roof of the ATP-binding pocket.

claim: I1084H mutation clashes with crizotinib's hinge-binding and solvent-front moieties without interfering with bound-ATP.

claim: Inhibitors were added at a concentration range of 0-10 µM (twofold dilutions) for dose-response experiments.

claim: 6 million cells were spinfected at an MOI of 0.1 in triplicate to generate the DMS transduced cell lines.

claim: Infected cells were selected with 1 μg/ml puromycin in 4 days.
source: Then infected cells were selected with 1 μg/ml puromycin in 4 days, with fluorescence and cell counts tracked each day.

claim: A total of 6 million cells from each replicate was harvested and pelleted at 250 x g to serve as the 'time point 0' pre-selection sample (T0).

claim: Time points were harvested every two doublings (~72 hr) across 12 days.
source: Time points were harvested every two doublings (~72 hr) across 12 days; 6 million cells were harvested for each condition and pelleted at 250 x g for 5 min; 2.0e5 cells/ml were split at every time point and maintained either in DMSO or TKI at the appropriate concentration to maintain cellular growth rates under inhibitor selection.

claim: The gDNA of each time point sample was isolated with the TakaraBio NucleoSpin Blood QuickPure kit the same day the cells were harvested.

claim: The PCR master mix for each sample was split into three PCR tubes with 50 μl volumes for each condition and amplified with 24 cycles.
source: The PCR master mix for each sample was split into three PCR tubes with 50 μl volumes for each condition and amplified with the following thermocycler parameters: initial denaturation at 98 °C for 30 s, followed by 24 x cycles of denaturation at 98 °C for 10 s, annealing at 60 °C for 15 s, extension at 68 °C for 14 s, and a final extension at 68 °C for 1 min.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: The entire 150 μl PCR reaction for each sample was mixed with 1X NEB Purple Loading Dye and run on a 0.8% agarose, 1X TBE gel.
source: The entire 150 μl PCR reaction for each sample was mixed with 1 X NEB Purple Loading Dye (6 X stock) and run on a 0.8% agarose, 1 X TBE gel, at 100 mA until there was clear ladder separation and distinct amplicon bands.

claim: Libraries were prepared for deep sequencing using the Nextera XT DNA Library Prep kit in a 96-well plate format.

claim: The library was paired-end sequenced (SP300) on two lanes of a NovaSeq6000.
